title: How to start selling on Amazon US in 2026: the complete beginner's guide
description: Start selling on Amazon.com in 2026: $39.99 plan, 2026–2027 FBA fees, sales tax, tariffs after de minimis, CPSC rules and your first 90 days.
tldr: Professional plan is $39.99/month; Individual is $0.99 per unit sold and can't run ads [s1].
Third-party sellers sold about 61% of paid units on Amazon in Q4 2025: it's a big but professional market [s21].
FBA fees rose ~$0.08/unit on Jan 15, 2026, a 3.5% fuel surcharge started Apr 17, 2026, and another ~$0.19/unit rise starts Jan 15, 2027 [s5][s7][s47].
Most categories pay a 15% referral fee [s46]; on a $25 kitchen item Amazon's fees come to about $10 (example using a reported FBA rate) [s10].
Amazon stopped prepping and labelling US FBA inventory on Jan 1, 2026; you must do it [s49].
De minimis duty-free entry ended for all countries on Aug 29, 2025; tariffs changed again in 2026, so get a current duty quote [s33][s36].
Amazon collects sales tax in marketplace facilitator states; most states' economic nexus threshold is $100,000 [s41][s40].
Payouts are held until 7 days after delivery (DD+7), so keep a cash buffer [s42].

blocks.p: Amazon.com is still the biggest and most competitive Amazon store in the world. Most of what you buy there is not sold by Amazon itself. **Third-party sellers** (independent businesses like the one you are about to start) sold about **61% of paid units in Q4 2025**, after 62% in Q3 2025, according to Amazon's own quarterly disclosures as summarised by AMZ Monitor [s21]. In plain terms: roughly six out of ten things shipped from Amazon come from sellers like you.

Seller counts are harder to pin down because Amazon does not publish them. Marketplace Pulse, a marketplace research firm, estimates that active sellers fell from about **2.4 million** in 2021 to about **1.65 million** at the end of 2025, and that only about **165,000** new sellers launched their first listing on Amazon.com in 2025, down 44% from 2024 and the lowest in a decade [s50]. Treat these as estimates. The direction matters more than the exact number: fewer new sellers are joining, but the ones already there are larger, more professional and better funded.

Amazon raised US FBA (Fulfilment by Amazon, where Amazon stores, packs and ships your stock) fees again on **January 15, 2026**, by about **$0.08 per unit on average** [s5]. It added a **3.5% fuel and logistics surcharge** on FBA fees from **April 17, 2026** [s7], and in November 2026 it announced another average rise of about **$0.19 per unit** from **January 15, 2027**, with the surcharge staying in place [s47]. There was no increase in referral fees (Amazon's commission on each sale) or FBA fees in 2025 [s5]. Each fee change on its own is small. Together they mean your margin plan must be built on next year's fees, not this year's.

Advertising is the other big cost. Amazon does not publish average cost-per-click (CPC, the price you pay each time a shopper clicks your ad) figures, and the numbers quoted online vary widely by category, so this guide does not quote one. Check the suggested bids for your own keywords inside the Amazon Ads console before you set a budget.

blocks.h3: AI shopping: Rufus changes how shoppers find products

blocks.p: **Rufus** is Amazon's AI shopping assistant: shoppers type or say a question ("best stroller for a small car boot") and Rufus answers with products. On the Q3 2025 earnings call Amazon said 250 million customers used Rufus that year and that it was on track for more than **$10 billion** in extra annualised sales [s23]. Amazon later said Rufus drove nearly **$12 billion** in incremental annualised sales in 2025 [s24]. In April 2026 Amazon said monthly Rufus users were up **115%** year over year [s25] and described Rufus as able to research products, track prices and buy automatically when a price target is hit [s26].

Amazon also sells ads inside these conversations, called **sponsored prompts**: suggested questions that appear in search results and on product pages. Amazon said nearly **20%** of shoppers who interact with a brand prompt continue the conversation about that brand [s26]. What this means for you: your listing has to answer real questions in plain language (size, use, who it is for, what is in the box), because an AI is now reading it on the shopper's behalf.

**Amazon Haul** is Amazon's low-price section built to compete with Temu. It launched with price ceilings of up to **$20**, and the direct-from-China route is still **invitation-only**. Since 2026 Amazon also cross-lists select low-priced products already stored in FBA into Haul, and Haul products now appear in Amazon's main search results; sellers can only opt their whole account out, not single products [s51]. Marketplace Pulse counts about 184,000 sellers with Haul listings in November 2026, with a median price of $9.98 [s51]. For a beginner, Haul is mostly a warning sign: if your product idea is a cheap, generic item, you are competing with ultra-low-cost sellers on price alone.

blocks.h3: What this means for a beginner

ul: The US is the largest prize, but it is a professional market. Plan to compete on a real brand, real product differences and good listings, not on finding an empty niche.
Build your numbers on 2027 fees, include the fuel surcharge, and leave room for advertising.
Write listings for humans and for AI: clear answers, real use cases, no keyword stuffing.
Avoid cheap commodity products that Haul and overseas marketplaces sell for less.

callout.title: The short version
callout.text: Amazon.com is big, mature and getting more expensive. It still rewards sellers who pick a differentiated product, price it with honest fee math, and keep stock in.

callout.title: Biggest operational change
callout.text: Since January 1, 2026 Amazon no longer preps or labels inventory for you in the US [s49]. Your supplier or a prep centre must apply barcode labels and any required bagging before stock ships.

sections.title: Is Amazon.com the right place for you to start?

ul: You live in the US or can legally operate a US business, with a US bank account and a valid card.
You have a product with a clear difference (better design, bundle, niche use) and margin after fees and ads.
You can fund at least one full inventory order plus three months of advertising without needing the payouts back quickly (remember DD+7 [s42]).
You are ready to handle sales tax, product safety documents and, if you import, customs.
Your idea is a cheap generic item under $20 that sells on price alone (you will compete with Haul and overseas sellers [s51]).
Your margin only works on this year's fees, before the 3.5% surcharge [s7] and the 2027 increase [s47].
Your product is for children, is electrical, edible or applied to skin, and you have no plan for testing and certificates.
You need the money back within a few weeks.

blocks.h3: Selling from outside the US (India, China and elsewhere)

blocks.p: Amazon.com accepts sellers from many countries. You register with your home-country ID and business documents and go through the same identity verification [s3]. What changes is money, tax and shipping:

ul: **Payouts:** you need a bank account that can receive USD payouts. Amazon's registration guide asks for a bank account and a card during sign-up, and says you do not need a US bank account: the Amazon Currency Converter can pay out to a supported bank outside the US [s3]. Some non-US sellers use a US-dollar receiving account instead; compare the conversion fees.

**US tax forms:** non-US sellers complete Amazon's tax interview with the non-US form (W-8BEN for individuals, W-8BEN-E for entities). Whether you owe US income tax depends on your country's tax treaty and how you operate; ask a cross-border accountant.

**Customs:** if you ship stock from India or China, someone must be the **importer of record** (the party responsible for paying duty and meeting import rules). Amazon is not your importer. Since August 29, 2025 low-value shipments no longer enter duty-free [s33], so every shipment needs a proper entry.

**Tariffs:** rates changed several times in 2025–2026 and more changes were reported as this guide was written [s36][s37][s39]. Get a current duty quote from a licensed customs broker for your product's HTS code (the customs classification number) before you order.

callout.title: Don't plan on the old cheap parcel model
callout.text: Shipping individual orders from China or India to US buyers duty-free is over [s33][s34]. Plan on bulk freight into FBA or a US warehouse, with duty paid at entry.

You upload your ID and proof of address, then either take a photo of your face with your ID or join or schedule a **video call** with an Amazon associate [s1]. Amazon says verification usually takes **three business days or less** [s3]. Seller forum guidance says to upload scanned or photographed originals (not screenshots) and keep total uploads under **50 MB** [s4].

blocks.h3: Common reasons for rejection or delay

ul: **Name or address mismatch** between your ID, statement and the form. This is the most common cause of rejection [s44].
Expired ID or a statement older than 180 days [s1].
Screenshots, cropped images or edited PDFs instead of clear originals [s4].
A bank account that is not in your name or your business's name [s3].
Opening a second account, or using a device or address linked to a suspended account.

blocks.p: Plan on one to three weeks from sign-up to a verified account if your documents are clean: the form itself takes an hour or two, verification usually takes up to three business days [s3], and the video call slot and any re-upload add time. Use that waiting time to finalise your product, barcodes and listing content.

sections.title: Every cost of selling on Amazon.com

blocks.p: Amazon publishes its fees in Seller Central and on its pricing pages. Plan prices and referral fees below come from Amazon's pricing page [s46]. FBA, storage and other fee figures come from Amazon notices where available and otherwise from 2026 rate-card summaries by trade sources; use them for planning and check the live numbers with Amazon's **Revenue Calculator** before you buy stock.

sections.title: Tax and legal basics in the US

blocks.h3: Sales tax and marketplace facilitator laws

blocks.p: The US has no national VAT. Instead, most states charge **sales tax**. Under **marketplace facilitator laws**, the marketplace (Amazon) calculates, collects and remits sales tax on orders it processes in those states, so you normally do not collect it yourself on Amazon orders [s41]. You still need to know where you have **nexus** (a tax connection to a state).

**Economic nexus** is triggered by selling more than a state's threshold into it. As of 2026, 41 states use **$100,000** in sales, Alabama and Mississippi use **$250,000**, and California, New York and Texas use **$500,000** [s40]. Some states also count transactions, but several have dropped that test: Illinois removed its 200-transaction test from **January 1, 2026** [s40]. **Physical nexus** can also come from inventory: FBA stores your stock in warehouses in many states, which can create nexus there.

ul: If you only sell on Amazon, Amazon handles collection in facilitator states [s41]. Some states still expect a registration or a return even when all your sales are through a marketplace; check each state's department of revenue.
If you also sell on your own website or other channels, those sales may require you to register and collect yourself once you cross a threshold [s40].
Thresholds and rules change; confirm on each state's revenue department site.
**US sellers:** a business entity (often an LLC) is optional but common; an **EIN** (Employer Identification Number) from the IRS lets you open a business bank account and file business taxes.

**Non-US sellers:** complete Amazon's tax interview with the right W-8 form. Some foreign sellers get an EIN or ITIN for tax treaty claims or US filings; a cross-border accountant can tell you whether you need one.
**Importers:** the importer of record needs a customs bond and usually a customs broker. Since the end of de minimis, every commercial import needs a formal or informal entry with duty paid [s33].

blocks.p: Your profit (sales minus Amazon fees, product cost, freight, duty, ads and other expenses) is taxable income. Amazon sends a Form 1099-K reporting your gross payments when you pass the IRS reporting threshold; check the current threshold on irs.gov because it has changed several times. Keep every invoice and your Amazon settlement reports from day one.

ul: Before you form a company or import your first order.
If you are a non-US seller (treaty and US filing questions).
When your sales pass about $100,000 into any one state, or you add a non-Amazon channel [s40].
If you paid IEEPA tariffs in 2025–2026, to ask about refunds [s36][s37].

callout.title: This is not tax advice
callout.text: Rules differ by state and by your home country. Use this as a map, then confirm with your state's department of revenue, the IRS and a qualified accountant.

sections.title: Product compliance, restrictions and Brand Registry

blocks.p: Some categories and products need Amazon's approval before you can list ("gated"), and some are banned. Before you choose a product, search the product type in Seller Central (Add a Product) to see if it shows "approval required". Common gated or restricted areas include grocery, topicals and supplements, children's products, some electronics, pesticides and anything making medical claims. Approval usually needs invoices from a legitimate supplier and safety documents.

The **Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC)** sets mandatory rules for many consumer products. Products designed for children need a **Children's Product Certificate (CPC)** based on testing by a **CPSC-accepted third-party lab**. Many other regulated products need a **General Certificate of Conformity (GCC)**. Amazon asks for these documents in Seller Central and can remove listings without them. CPSC has also moved certificate data to electronic filing with customs for imports, so if you import regulated products, ask your customs broker and lab about eFiling before your goods ship. Check cpsc.gov for the current requirements for your product.

ul: Children's products, toys, baby gear: CPC, lab test reports, tracking labels.
Electrical items: safety testing and, for radio devices, FCC rules.
Cosmetics, food contact items, supplements: FDA rules and labelling.
Products with batteries, aerosols or flammables: dangerous goods (hazmat) review before FBA will accept them.
English labelling, country of origin marking for imports, and any warnings your product's rules require.
An FBA barcode label (FNSKU) or eligible manufacturer barcode on each unit. Since Jan 1, 2026 you must apply labels yourself or through a prep centre [s49].
Don't make claims you can't prove ("FDA approved", "antibacterial", "non-toxic") without documentation; these trigger listing removals.

blocks.p: **Amazon Brand Registry** gives you control of your listings, A+ content, Brand Store, Vine, Sponsored Brands ads and brand protection tools. It requires a registered or pending trademark from an eligible office; in the US that is the **USPTO** (United States Patent and Trademark Office). Brand Registry accepts a **pending** or registered trademark, so file early [s3]. Registration itself can take many months; check the USPTO's current processing-time page for an up-to-date estimate.

Amazon's **IP Accelerator** connects brands with vetted IP law firms at pre-negotiated rates and can give earlier access to Brand Registry protections while the trademark is pending. It is optional; any qualified trademark attorney can file for you.

callout.title: Do this first
callout.text: File your word mark (brand name) before you place your first inventory order. Then you can apply for Brand Registry as soon as you have the application serial number.

sections.title: Choosing your first product with data

ul: **Price $20–$50.** High enough to cover fees and ads; the worked example shows Amazon fees take about 40% of a $25 item [s10][s46].
**Small and light.** Small standard and light large standard tiers keep FBA fees down [s10]. Every extra pound and inch costs you, and 2027 raises small-standard fees the most [s47].
**Steady, year-round demand.** Avoids being stuck with stock and paying $2.40 per cubic foot in Q4 storage [s12].
**A real improvement** you can explain in one sentence, which also helps AI assistants recommend you [s26].
**Not gated, not regulated** (for your first product), no batteries, liquids or claims.
**Reviews you can beat:** top sellers have complaints you can fix (read their 1–3 star reviews).

blocks.p: Aim for at least **30% net margin before ads** and a landed cost (product + freight + duty + prep) of no more than about a quarter of your price. Using the worked example ($25 item, $10.06 Amazon fees): if landed cost is $6, you keep $8.94 before storage, returns and ads, about 36% [s10][s46]. If your margin is thin at today's fees, add the 2027 increase [s47] and the current tariff for your product before deciding.

blocks.h3: Validating demand with Amazon's own tools

ul: **Product Opportunity Explorer** (Seller Central): search volume, growth, number of products, average price and return rates by niche.
**Brand Analytics** (after Brand Registry): top search terms and which products win clicks and sales.
**Revenue Calculator**: test fees on similar products by size and price.
**Amazon Ads console**: suggested bids for your main keywords, which tell you what traffic will cost.
Read Rufus answers for your category questions as a shopper, to see which products and features it highlights [s23].
Seasonal (Christmas, Halloween, summer only).
Fragile (glass, ceramics) or heavy/oversize.
Patented or trademarked designs you might infringe; search patents before ordering.
Children's, electrical, food, cosmetics or supplements as a first product (compliance cost and risk).
Under $15 commodity items competing with Haul [s51].
Categories where the top listings all have thousands of reviews and the same Chinese factories behind them.
High tariff exposure from a single country with no alternative supplier [s39].

callout.title: Don't copy, improve
callout.text: Selling an identical copy of a branded product invites IP complaints and price wars. Change something meaningful and protect it with your own brand.

Reviews at a healthy rating, conversion improving, ads ACoS trending down, reorder placed.
Organic sales growing, TACoS falling, price near target, a clear plan for product two.

ul: **Sponsored Products**: ads for a single listing in search results and on product pages. Start here.
**Sponsored Brands**: headline ads with your logo and several products (needs Brand Registry).
**Sponsored Display**: retargeting and product-page ads, on and off Amazon.
**Sponsored prompts**: ads inside Rufus conversations, a newer format [s26].
**ACoS** (Advertising Cost of Sale) = ad spend ÷ ad sales. $30 spend for $100 ad sales = 30% ACoS.
**TACoS** (Total ACoS) = ad spend ÷ total sales (ads + organic). Shows whether ads are building organic sales.
**Break-even ACoS** = your margin before ads. In the $25 example with a $6 landed cost, margin before ads is about 36%, so ACoS above 36% loses money on each ad sale [s10][s46].

ol: **Auto campaign**: Amazon chooses targets. Use it to discover search terms.
**Manual exact**: your 5–15 most relevant keywords.
**Manual phrase/broad**: wider versions to find new terms.
**Product targeting**: your listing on competitor pages where you have a clear advantage.

blocks.p: Set the daily budget from real bids: take the suggested bid for your main keywords in the Ads console, decide how many clicks you need per day (at a 10% conversion rate, 10 clicks ≈ 1 sale), and multiply. Keep the total within what you can afford for 60–90 days.

ul: Days 1–30: expect ACoS above your break-even. You are buying data and early sales.
Days 30–60: bring ACoS toward break-even on proven keywords.
Day 90+: aim for ACoS below break-even and a falling TACoS.

ol: Download the search term report.
Add negatives: irrelevant terms and terms with many clicks and no sales.
Move converting search terms into exact campaigns.
Adjust bids: up on profitable terms, down on expensive ones.
Check budget: campaigns running out of budget early in the day.
Look at TACoS and organic rank, not just ACoS.

ul: **Amazon Vine** for early honest reviews (Brand Registry).
**Request a Review** button or automation in Seller Central, which sends Amazon's standard request.
Product inserts may thank the buyer and point to support, but never ask for a positive review or offer anything in return.
Fix the product when reviews show a real problem; it raises rating faster than any tactic.
**Brand Store**: a free multi-page store on Amazon.
**A+ Content** and **Brand Analytics** for search and competitor insight.
**Sponsored Brands** ads to drive traffic to your store.

sections.title: The most common beginner mistakes (and account-health risks)

ol: **Picking a product on hype, not math.** Run the fee math with 2027 fees, the 3.5% surcharge and current tariffs first [s7][s47][s39].
**Underfunding cash flow.** Payouts are held until 7 days after delivery [s42]; plan for it.
**Mismatched documents during sign-up.** Name and address must match everywhere [s44].
**Opening a second account** without Amazon's approval, or logging in from a device tied to a suspended account. This can link and suspend both.
**Shipping unlabelled or unprepped stock.** Amazon no longer preps in the US [s49].
**Stocking out** after launch, then losing rank and paying low-inventory fees [s16].
**Over-ordering** before demand is proven, then paying Q4 and aged storage [s12].
**Review manipulation**: paying for reviews, rebates in exchange for reviews, friends-and-family reviews, review swaps. These lead to suspension and listing removal.
**Listing restricted or unsafe products** without certificates (children's products, electrical, supplements).
**Copying a branded design** and receiving IP (trademark, patent, copyright) complaints, which damage account health.
**Selling items as "new" without supplier invoices**; inauthentic complaints need proof of authentic sourcing.
**Ignoring tariffs and the importer-of-record role** when importing [s33][s36].
**FBM late shipments and cancellations**, which harm performance metrics and Buy Box (the 'Add to Cart' box) eligibility.
**Ignoring Account Health** in Seller Central. Check it daily; respond to every notification before its deadline.
**Keyword-stuffed listings** that read badly for humans and for Rufus [s26].

callout.title: What gets accounts suspended
callout.text: Fake or incentivised reviews, multiple accounts, unverifiable identity, inauthentic or counterfeit goods, unsafe products and repeated IP complaints. None of these are worth the risk.

faq.q: How much does it cost to start selling on Amazon in the US?
faq.a: The Professional plan is $39.99 a month, plus referral fees (usually 15%) and FBA fees per unit. The big costs are inventory, freight, duty, photos and launch ads, which depend on your product. Build a budget from supplier quotes and suggested ad bids rather than a generic number.

Individual costs $0.99 per item sold and has no monthly fee, but you can't run ads. Professional is $39.99 a month. If you sell more than about 40 units a month or want to advertise and build a brand, choose Professional.

faq.q: Can I sell on Amazon.com from India or China?
faq.a: Yes. You register with your home documents, pass identity verification, and complete a W-8BEN or W-8BEN-E tax form. You will need a way to receive USD payouts and someone to act as importer of record for your shipments, since US de minimis duty-free entry has ended.

faq.q: Do I have to collect sales tax on Amazon?
faq.a: Generally no for Amazon orders: under marketplace facilitator laws Amazon collects and remits sales tax in states with those laws. You still need to watch for nexus if you sell through other channels, and confirm any state registration rules with an accountant.

faq.q: What are Amazon's FBA fees in 2026?
faq.a: They depend on size, weight and price band. Trade-source rate cards put a $10–$50 small standard unit up to 2 oz at about $3.32 and a large standard unit of 2.25–2.5 lb at about $6.10, before the 3.5% fuel surcharge; confirm in Amazon's Revenue Calculator. Fees rise again on January 15, 2027 by about $0.19 per unit on average.

faq.q: How long does Amazon seller verification take?
faq.a: Amazon says identity verification usually takes three business days or less once you submit documents or finish the video call. Delays usually come from name or address mismatches or old statements, so make everything match before you start.

faq.q: Do I need a trademark to sell on Amazon?
faq.a: Not to sell, but you need one (registered or pending) for Brand Registry, which unlocks A+ content, Vine, Sponsored Brands and brand protection. File with the USPTO early because registration can take many months.

faq.q: How did tariffs and the end of de minimis change things?
faq.a: Since August 29, 2025 low-value imports from all countries need proper customs entries and duty. Tariff rates changed several times in 2026 after the Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs, and new increases were reported in November 2026. Get a current duty quote before each order.

faq.q: Does Amazon still label and prep my FBA inventory?
faq.a: No. Since January 1, 2026 Amazon no longer offers prep and item labelling for US FBA shipments. Your supplier or a prep centre must label and pack each unit to Amazon's rules.

faq.q: How long until I get paid by Amazon?
faq.a: Under the DD+7 policy, money from a sale becomes available seven days after Amazon confirms delivery, then goes out in your next disbursement. Plan for a few weeks between a sale and cash in your bank.

faq.q: What is a good ACoS for a new product?
faq.a: In the first month ACoS is often above break-even while you gather data. Your break-even ACoS equals your margin before ads; for example about 36% on a $25 product with $10 of Amazon fees and $6 landed cost. Aim to get below break-even by day 60–90.

faq.q: What is Rufus and does it affect my listing?
faq.a: Rufus is Amazon's AI shopping assistant, used by hundreds of millions of shoppers and credited by Amazon with about $12 billion in extra sales in 2025. It reads your listing to answer shoppers' questions, so write clear, specific answers about use, size and who the product is for.
Use Amazon Vine and the Request a Review button. Never pay for reviews, give refunds or gifts for reviews, or ask friends and family; Amazon suspends accounts for review manipulation.

You can't simply sign up: the direct-from-China route is invitation-only, and Amazon itself cross-lists select low-priced FBA products into Haul (you can opt your whole account out). For most beginners a differentiated branded product in the main store is a better bet.
